**(B)** histology

The study of the structure and arrangement of tissues is called histology; Bichat is known as the 'Father of Histology'. Anatomy is the study of internal structure in general, microbiology is the study of microorganisms, and morphology is the study of external form.

**(C)** Pancreas

The pancreas is a mixed gland: its exocrine part pours pancreatic juice through a duct into the intestine, and its islets of Langerhans release hormones such as insulin and glucagon directly into the blood. Sebaceous and mammary glands are only exocrine (duct-bearing), and the pituitary is only endocrine (ductless).

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives the pancreas as the gland that is both exocrine and endocrine.]

**(B)** Hemidesmosomes

Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells firmly to the underlying basement membrane, and this cell-to-matrix attachment is made by integrin proteins. Desmosomes and adherens junctions join cell to cell using cadherins, and gap junctions are channels formed by connexins.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives integrins as the linking proteins of hemidesmosomes.]

**(C)** chondrin

The matrix of cartilage is called chondrin, in which chondrocytes lie in lacunae. Ossein is the hard matrix of bone, haemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying pigment of red blood cells, and renin is an enzyme from the kidney, not a cartilage protein.

**(D)** Salivary gland

The salivary gland is an exocrine gland: it pours saliva through a duct to a specific site. The thyroid, pituitary and adrenal glands are endocrine (ductless) glands that release hormones directly into the blood, so the salivary gland is the odd one out.

[Note: the chapter names thyroid and pituitary as endocrine but not the adrenal; standard biology gives the adrenal as an endocrine gland too.]
